stages.title: News watchlist: 11 changes worth following
stages.summary: Open protocols, platform access, agent payments, personalized pricing, and AI transparency. Each item links to a company or regulatory source recorded in the original run.
stages.callout: Selected comparison: Amazon and Shopify combine in-house capabilities, third-party access, and permission controls differently. Neither is simply fully open or fully closed.

cards.title: Google introduces the Universal Commerce Protocol
cards.text: Google, with Shopify, Etsy, Wayfair, Target, and Walmart, introduces an open commerce protocol covering discovery, purchasing, and post-purchase services, compatible with A2A, AP2, and MCP.
cards.signal: Could control over open standards redistribute bargaining power among platforms, merchants, and payment providers?

cards.title: Walmart products enter Gemini
cards.text: Walmart and Sam's Club products are set to enter Gemini through UCP, moving the shopping entry point from retail websites to a general-purpose AI interface.
cards.signal: When transactions begin on an AI platform, who controls customer relationships, recommendations, and data?

cards.title: Amazon's Agent Policy takes effect
cards.text: Amazon requires automated agents accessing services on sellers' behalf to identify themselves and comply with policies; it may require them to stop accessing its services.
cards.signal: When do platforms treat third-party agents as complementary innovators, and when as entrants requiring control?

cards.title: Amazon expands Seller Assistant
cards.text: Amazon reports that Seller Assistant supports operational advice, diagnosis, and action planning, with 230,000 monthly users in the saved source record.
cards.signal: When a platform both sets market rules and advises sellers, are its objectives aligned with sellers' interests?

cards.title: Shopify launches Agentic Storefronts
cards.text: Shopify connects millions of merchants' products, inventory, and prices to AI channels such as ChatGPT while retaining merchant fulfillment relationships.
cards.signal: Does access to multiple AI channels increase merchant reach or create new dependence on intermediaries?

cards.title: Shopify opens UCP and the Catalog API
cards.text: Developers can use UCP and the Catalog API without applying for approval and submit agent profiles through a public MCP endpoint.
cards.signal: Can lower entry barriers support specialized agents and pressure closed platforms to change their policies?

cards.title: ChatGPT expands product discovery and comparison
cards.text: ChatGPT extends ACP to product discovery, supporting visual browsing, side-by-side comparisons, and more timely product information.
cards.signal: How could AI-interface rankings affect brand exposure, price competition, and search advertising?

cards.title: Visa launches Intelligent Commerce Connect
cards.text: Visa offers an access layer for agent developers, merchants, and payment providers and begins initial partner pilots.
cards.signal: Could identity, authorization, and payment liability become bottlenecks or entry barriers in agentic commerce?

cards.title: Google transfers AP2 to the FIDO Alliance
cards.text: Google transfers governance of the Agent Payments Protocol to the FIDO Alliance and adds authorization capabilities for unattended transactions.
cards.signal: Why would a firm relinquish protocol control? Could neutral governance accelerate ecosystem adoption?

cards.title: EU AI transparency requirements begin to apply
cards.text: The saved record describes transparency requirements for specified AI systems and AI-generated content, with implications for interfaces and disclosure design.
cards.signal: Does disclosing AI involvement improve trust or reduce advice adoption and conversion?

cards.title: FTC seeks comments on personalized pricing enforcement
cards.text: The saved record describes an FTC consultation on potential legal risks from undisclosed use of personal data in personalized pricing, with comments due September 18, 2026.
cards.signal: How does regulatory uncertainty affect firms' use of consumer data and personalized prices?

stages.title: What conditions favor each governance mode?
stages.summary: Six candidate mechanisms predict in-house provision, open access, or selective access.
stages.callout: The question is not simply open versus closed: it is how platforms balance control benefits, external innovation, and safety risks.

cards.title: H1 · Data advantages favor in-house provision
cards.text: More distinctive transaction, fulfillment, and user data may improve an in-house agent's predictions and strengthen the incentive to retain decision capabilities internally.

cards.title: H2 · Complementary-service profits favor in-house provision
cards.text: When advertising, logistics, or payment services are profitable, an in-house agent can coordinate recommendations and service adoption, potentially favoring internal provision.

cards.title: H3 · External innovation favors open access
cards.text: Greater third-party expertise and innovation efficiency increase the value of tool variety and may favor access by multiple agents.

cards.title: H4 · Merchant heterogeneity favors open access
cards.text: A single platform agent may struggle to serve heterogeneous needs. Specialized third-party agents can match different industries, firm sizes, and operating objectives.

cards.title: H5 · Risk favors selective access
cards.text: When external innovation is valuable but execution errors, data leakage, and liability are substantial, certification, tiered permissions, and audits may outperform either unrestricted access or exclusive in-house provision.

cards.title: H6 · Platform competition favors openness commitments
cards.text: When platforms compete for merchants, admitting third-party agents may credibly reduce lock-in, expand choice, and attract merchants.

stages.title: Three trade-offs shape governance choices
stages.summary: Control and internalization, ecosystem innovation and matching, and safety and liability are three dimensions of institutional choice.
stages.callout: Selective access is a distinct regime: certification, permissions, and audits enable external innovation while retaining key controls.

cards.title: Trade-off A · Control and internalization
cards.text: Data advantages and complementary-service profits raise the value of in-house provision and control over agent objectives, default recommendations, and data feedback.

cards.title: Trade-off B · Innovation and ecosystem scale
cards.text: Third-party innovation, specialized matching, and competition for merchants raise the value of openness. A platform trades some control for a richer ecosystem.

cards.title: Trade-off C · Risk and reliable execution
cards.text: Operational errors, privacy breaches, and liability raise the cost of access. Certification and tiered permissions screen third parties while preserving innovation.

cards.title: Unifying question
cards.text: When does a platform choose in-house provision, open access, or selective access? Compare control benefits, innovation value, and risk-management capabilities across regimes.

stages.title: From related findings to a provisional research question
stages.summary: Platform governance, algorithmic pricing, and advice adoption have close precedents. Price effects or adoption alone may offer limited novelty.
stages.callout: Provisional opportunity: compare in-house provision, open access, and selective access in one model of endogenous platform governance. This is a search-dependent conjecture, not an established gap.

cards.title: Teh (2022) · Platform Governance
cards.text: The saved audit connects this paper's account of rules, information, and recommendations to seller competition. It proposes agent provision and certified access as a possible extension requiring further overlap checks.

cards.title: Calvano et al. (2020) · Algorithmic Pricing
cards.text: Autonomous pricing algorithms can sustain supracompetitive prices. Price convergence or collusion alone is therefore unlikely to establish a distinctive contribution.

cards.title: Brown & MacKay (2023) · Pricing Algorithms
cards.text: Automated responses and pricing frequency affect price levels and dispersion. Changes in prices following openness are outcomes to explain, not by themselves a novel contribution.

cards.title: Greiner et al. (2025) · Algorithmic Advice
cards.text: Incentive contracts and the framing of AI affect managers' adoption of advice. The saved audit treats this as a foundation for seller reliance and flags the advice provider's strategic objectives for closer comparison.

cards.title: Keppo et al. (2026) · Trusting AI in Competitive Markets
cards.text: This preprint is recorded as directly studying AI pricing advice, trust learning, and competition. The original audit therefore rejects a generic question about whether AI advice changes prices.

cards.title: Provisional differentiation
cards.text: The original search did not identify a paper directly modeling endogenous choice among all three regimes. This is a preliminary search result, not proof of novelty; a dedicated follow-up search remains necessary.

stages.title: Reviewer: governance is endogenous and multidimensional
stages.summary: Key concerns include regime classification, platform heterogeneity, bundled policies, data visibility, and what agents add beyond ordinary recommendation systems.
stages.callout: Amazon and Shopify cannot be treated as closed and open treatment groups. Both may use mixed governance, and their choices reflect their own characteristics.

cards.title: Major 1 · Open versus closed is insufficient
cards.text: A platform may provide its own agent, open some interfaces, and restrict high-risk actions simultaneously. Define governance through entry, data, permissions, review, and liability.

cards.title: Major 2 · Governance is endogenous
cards.text: Data advantages, revenue models, merchant heterogeneity, and risk exposure jointly affect governance and outcomes. Cross-platform differences alone do not identify causal effects.

cards.title: Major 3 · Policies change together
cards.text: Agent-access changes often coincide with recommendation, payment, advertising, or data-policy changes. A single event may not isolate the effect of governance.

cards.title: Major 4 · Key behavior is unobserved
cards.text: External researchers typically cannot observe agent advice, permissions, adoption, or execution logs. An empirical study may require a data partnership or an experimental alternative.

cards.title: Alternative explanation · Safety, not self-preferencing
cards.text: Restrictions may prevent execution errors, data leakage, and spillover liability. The model must allow genuine safety benefits rather than assume the platform's motives.

cards.title: Feasible revision
cards.text: Use a three-regime theoretical model to explain governance choice, then controlled experiments to test objective conflicts and permission design. Platform news motivates the question but does not identify causal effects.

stages.title: Governance choice ranks first among four candidates
stages.summary: The three-regime question combines observed variation with theoretical trade-offs and candidate comparative statics. Price and capability effects become secondary outcomes.
stages.callout: Ask why platforms choose different institutions; do not interpret cross-platform outcome differences as causal effects of openness.

cards.title: #1 In-house, open, or selective access?
cards.text: A common model of platform control, ecosystem innovation, and safety risk could yield distinct equilibrium regimes and testable shifts in their boundaries.

cards.title: #2 How do an agent provider's objectives shape advice?
cards.text: Objective conflicts are clear and experimentally tractable, but explain downstream consequences rather than the platform's choice of regime.

cards.title: #3 Does openness narrow merchant capability gaps?
cards.text: The managerial relevance is clear, but adoption and developer entry are endogenous. Treat this as an extension involving merchant heterogeneity.

cards.title: #4 Does AI advice lead to price convergence?
cards.text: Testable, but closely related to algorithmic pricing, competitive responses, and trust in AI advice. Do not retain it as the core question.

stages.title: Proposed study: platform choice of agent governance
stages.summary: The object of study is the platform's choice among three regimes. Amazon and Shopify motivate the question rather than identify its causal effects.
stages.callout: CONDITIONAL GO: first test whether a three-regime model yields distinct equilibrium regions; only then commit to data collection or experiments.

cards.title: Research puzzle
cards.text: Under what conditions does a platform choose in-house agents, open third-party access, or selective access? How do these regimes distribute value among platforms, developers, and merchants?

cards.title: Three candidate regimes
cards.text: In-house: the platform controls the model, data, and permissions. Open: eligible developers may enter freely. Selective: certification, tiered permissions, and audits screen third-party agents.

cards.title: Minimal theoretical model
cards.text: Stage 1: the platform selects governance. Stage 2: third parties decide whether to enter and invest in innovation. Stage 3: merchants select agents and act. Platform payoffs include transactions, complementary services, and data, net of governance and safety costs.

cards.title: Conjectured regime predictions
cards.text: Data advantages or complementary-service profits may favor in-house provision; third-party innovation or merchant heterogeneity may favor openness. Valuable innovation with high risk and effective screening may favor selective access. These predictions remain to be derived.

cards.title: Conjectured downstream predictions
cards.text: Holding information and accuracy fixed, in-house agents may recommend more platform services; open access may increase specialization; selective access may reduce tail risks but also discourage third-party investment.

cards.title: Research design
cards.text: Use theory to explain regime choice. Randomize the agent provider, objective alignment, and execution permissions in controlled experiments to test downstream mechanisms. Platform news provides motivation, not cross-platform causal identification.

cards.title: No-go checks
cards.text: Stop if the regimes do not produce distinct equilibrium regions, agents introduce no delegation or execution features beyond ordinary APIs or recommendations, or a dedicated search finds the same institutional-choice problem already fully studied.
